newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: AFP WANT PERMITS FOR FUTURE PARLIAMENT HOUSE PROTESTS
The Parliamentary committee inquiry into the August riots at Canberra's parliament house has heard that issuing permits for such demonstrations may help control future incidents.
Dozens of Australian Federal Police Officers were injured during the union protests which got out of control.
Assistant AFP commissioner, Bill Stoll, says that while protests are usually organised and carried out with goodwill, permits could further emphasise the rules laid down for protests.
He says permits would give the organisers of the demonstrations the ability to tell those involved in the protests what the presiding officers have defined they are able to do.
AUSTRALIA TRYING TO PROTECT AGRICULTURE TRADE GAINS
Australia will be out to keep the gains it's made in agricultural international trade, when the World Trade Organisation holds its summit in Singapore next month.
The Trade Minister, Tim Fischer, says agreement was reached overnight on the terms of a 1999 review into trade in agriculture.
Mr Fischer says the Australian-led agricultural bloc - the Cairns Group - had already fought off attempts to water down farm-trade promises made in the Uruguay Round of trade talks.
BRYANT TO BE SENTENCED UNDER CHANGED LAWS
Recent changes to sentencing laws will give Tasmania's Chief Justice more flexibility in determining the sentence for self confessed Port Arthur gunman Martin Bryant.
Murder in Tasmania no longer carries a mandatory life sentence.
Bryant yesterday reversed his plea, confessing to 72 charges including 35 for murder at Port Arthur.
His sentence will be determined by Mr Justice Cox after a pre-sentence hearing starting on Tuesday week.
BANKS NOT WORRIED ABOUT NEW CREDIT CARD
The banking industry says it's reserving judgement on a new entry in the credit card market...despite claims the new card will offer interest rates up to three percent lower than the banks.
Aussie Home Loans hopes to duplicate its success with mortgages, when it launches a credit card product next year, possibly by February.
The non-bank lender says its involvement in the home loan market has forced bank margins on mortgages to drop from 4-and-a-half to 2-and-a-quarter percent.
CAUTION URGED DURING TRIPS TO COLOMBIA
Travellers to Colombia have been warned to exercise extreme caution and maintain a high level of personal security.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade says widespread guerilla activity, drug trafficking and common crime are prevalent in Colombia - the greater risk being in the rural areas.
The Department says travel outside major cities and tourist centres, especially by road, should be avoided.
ANZ STAFF THREATEN INDUSTRIAL ACTION
ANZ bank staff across the country are this morning calling on their employer to give them greater consideration in future planning.
Staff are warning of rolling stoppages unless the ANZ places an immediate moratorium on restructuring.
State secretary of the Finance Sector union, Mark Lynch, says the ANZ is trying to boost its share price by slashing 7000 jobs and closing 100 branches.
MCDONALD TAKES OVER NATIONALS' FEDERAL REINS
The former Queensland National Party president has been promoted to the top of the federal party hierarchy.
Don McDonald has been elected the new Federal National Party president.
He takes over from Western Australia's John Patterson who completed his term at the party's Federal Council in Canberra today.
Mr McDonald stood down from the state presidency last year and was elected senior vice president of the federal party.
RACE DEBATE SPARKING DISCRIMINATION COMPLAINTS
It's believed a big increase in race discrimination complaints in Australia could be linked to the current debate.

Race Discrimination Commissioner Zita Antonios says the number of formal complaints lodged with the Human Rights Commission doubled in the last quarter from July through to September compared to the previous three months.
ASC CLAIMS CREDIT FOR $16 MILLION RETURN
More than 16-million dollars has been returned to investors and creditors in the last financial year through the actions of the Australian Securities Commission.
ASC chairman Alan Camercon has picked out two 1980's cases as highlights of the 1995/96 year.
The Commission secured the criminal conviction of Alan Bond, who's in jail for three years on charges relating to the Manet painting "La Promenade".
And Duke Group director, Paul Fitzsimmons, received a two-year term after Kia Ora Gold was found to have funded its own takeover in 1988 to the tune of almost 12-million dollars.
In total, the financial year saw 19 corporate criminals go to jail as a result of ASC action.
